passages.happening:
With the theft dealt with, God speaks to Joshua again, and his first words are kind. “Do not be afraid or discouraged. Take the whole army with you, and go up and attack Ai. See, I have delivered into your hand the king of Ai, his people, his city, and his land” (verse 1).

Ai is to be treated as Jericho was, with one difference. This time Israel may keep the plunder and the livestock. And God gives a plan: “Set up an ambush behind the city” (verse 2).

Joshua sends a force by night to hide west of the city, between Ai and Bethel. He explains the trick. He will march on the city with the main army. When the men of Ai come out, Israel will run, as it did before. The defenders will think it is the first battle over again and chase them. Then the hidden men are to rise and take the empty city (verses 4-8).

In the morning Joshua and the elders lead the army up and camp north of Ai, with a valley between them and the town (verses 10-13).
passages.hearers:
The words ‘Do not be afraid or discouraged’ are the words God spoke to Joshua at the start of the book. After a defeat and an execution, Joshua needed to hear them again. God does not hold the failure of chapter 7 over him. Once the wrong has been put right, the promise is simply repeated.

The first attack on Ai went wrong from its first step. A few men were sent, on the scouts' advice, and no one asked God. This time God gives the order, and the whole army goes. The contrast is meant to be seen.

The plan is quite unlike Jericho. There are no horns and no falling wall. There is an ambush and a pretended retreat, which were ordinary tactics of ancient war. God gives the plan himself. The book does not think God works only through wonders. Here he works through a night march and careful planning, obeyed.

Israel's earlier defeat is turned into a tool. The men of Ai will come out boldly because they have beaten Israel once. What had been a shame becomes the bait.

The plunder is allowed this time. Not every city was under the full ban, and the law made room for that. The permission throws a sad light back on Achan. What he stole and hid at Jericho, he could have taken openly a few days later.

Joshua spends the night ‘among the people’ (verse 9). After chapter 7 the leader stays close to his men.
passages.later:
The law of Moses had given rules for plunder in some of Israel's wars (Deuteronomy 20:14). The note on that chapter says plainly what those rules allowed and does not defend it.

A proverb sets planning and trust side by side, as this chapter does: “A horse is prepared for the day of battle, but victory is of the LORD” (Proverbs 21:31).
passages.asks: After the failure God said again, ‘Do not be afraid or discouraged’, and sent Joshua back to the very place where he had lost. Ask where you failed and have not gone back. Ask whether what went wrong has been put right, and whether you can hear God give you the task again. And ask whether you only expect God in the unusual, or also in a careful plan faithfully carried out.

passages.t: The ambush, and the fall of Ai
passages.happening:
The king of Ai sees Israel and hurries out with his men at first light. “But he did not know that an ambush had been set up against him behind the city” (verse 14).

Israel lets itself be driven back and runs toward the wilderness. Every man in Ai, and in Bethel too, goes after them, ‘leaving the city wide open’ (verse 17).

Then the LORD says to Joshua, “Hold out your battle lance toward Ai, for into your hand I will deliver the city” (verse 18). Joshua holds it out. The hidden men rise, run in, and set the city on fire. The men of Ai look back and see smoke. Israel's main force turns on them, and they are caught between the two.

The chapter gives the number of the dead as twelve thousand, men and women (verse 25). “Joshua did not draw back the hand that held his battle lance until he had devoted to destruction all who lived in Ai” (verse 26). Israel takes the livestock and goods, as God had allowed.

Ai is burned and left ‘a permanent heap of ruins’ (verse 28). The king is put to death and his body hung on a tree until evening. At sunset Joshua has it taken down and laid at the city gate, and a heap of stones is raised over it (verse 29).
passages.hearers:
The battle is told with close attention to place and movement: north, west, behind, between. It reverses chapter 7 point by point. Israel runs from Ai again, and this time the running is the plan.

Joshua's raised lance is the signal to the men in hiding. It also recalls an older scene. When Israel fought Amalek in the wilderness, Moses stood on a hill with his hands lifted, and Joshua was the young commander below. Now Joshua is the one with the raised arm, and the meaning is the same. The victory is marked as the LORD's.

Verses 24 to 26 say that the people of Ai were killed, women as well as men, and the word for the ban is used. This is the same hard matter as Jericho. The note on chapter 6, verses 17 to 21, sets out the ways Christians read it and the cost of each, and what holds on every reading. It is not repeated here, and it is not softened here either. No one may use this chapter to justify violence against any person or people, and it has no nation, state, land or conflict of today in view.

The treatment of the king's body follows a law in Deuteronomy. A body hung up after death was a public sign of disgrace, and the law said it must not stay there overnight, so that the land would not be defiled. Joshua keeps that law in the middle of a war. Even a dead enemy's body is under God's rule and must be buried by evening.

The chapter ends this battle with a heap of stones over a king. The last chapter ended with a heap of stones over Achan. One was an Israelite and one a Canaanite, and the book sets the two heaps side by side.

Where Ai stood, and what has been found there, is debated. The book page sets out the views.
passages.later:
The law Joshua kept reads, ‘you must not leave the body on the tree overnight, but you must be sure to bury him that day, because anyone who is hung on a tree is under God’s curse’ (Deuteronomy 21:23).

Paul quotes that law when he writes about the cross: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us. For it is written: ‘Cursed is everyone who is hung on a tree.’” (Galatians 3:13). In Joshua the curse rests on a defeated king. Paul says that at the cross Christ took the curse on himself, for others.

The scene with Moses is in Exodus: “As long as Moses held up his hands, Israel prevailed; but when he lowered them, Amalek prevailed” (Exodus 17:11).
passages.hard:
Twelve thousand men and women are said to have died at Ai. How should a reader take that?

It is the same question as Jericho, and it deserves the same honesty. The text says that the people of the town were killed and uses the word for the ban.

Christians who receive this book as God's word read these reports in several ways. Some read them as God's judgment on the long sin of Canaan (Genesis 15:16), limited to that moment. Some read their sweeping language as the usual style of ancient reports of war, which this same book qualifies when it admits that many Canaanites remained. Some ground the command in God's right over life. Some read these texts as God meeting an ancient people within their understanding, to be read in the light of Christ. Many hold more than one together. The note on chapter 6 gives each reading with its cost. The site takes no side, and none of them makes the passage easy.

What holds on every reading was said there and is said again. This was tied to one land and one moment. It was never made a pattern. No one may use it to justify violence against any person or people.
passages.asks: Do not read the middle of this passage quickly. Ask what troubles you in it and bring that to God. Then look at two small things. Israel's old defeat became the means of its recovery. Ask whether God might use something you are ashamed of. And Joshua stopped at sunset to bury an enemy according to God's law. Ask how you treat people you have beaten in an argument or a contest once it is over.

passages.happening:
The scene changes completely. “At that time Joshua built an altar on Mount Ebal to the LORD, the God of Israel” (verse 30). He builds it as the law of Moses required, ‘an altar of uncut stones on which no iron tool has been used’ (verse 31). Burnt offerings and peace offerings are made on it.

There, in front of the people, Joshua writes a copy of the law of Moses on stones (verse 32).

All Israel stands in two halves, one in front of Mount Gerizim and one in front of Mount Ebal, with the ark and the priests between them. The writer notes who is there: ‘foreigners and citizens alike’ (verse 33).

Then Joshua reads. He reads all the words of the law, ‘the blessings and the curses’ (verse 34). “There was not a word of all that Moses had commanded that Joshua failed to read before the whole assembly of Israel, including the women, the little ones, and the foreigners who lived among them” (verse 35).
passages.hearers:
Moses had commanded exactly this. Before he died he told Israel that when they had crossed the Jordan they were to set up stones on Mount Ebal, write the law on them, build an altar of uncut stones, and stand on the two mountains while the promises and the warnings of the covenant were spoken. Joshua does each thing in turn. The phrase ‘as Moses the servant of the LORD had commanded’ is the thread of the passage.

Ebal and Gerizim stand on either side of a valley, with the old town of Shechem between them. Abraham had built his first altar in the land at Shechem. Israel is standing where the promise of the land was first spoken.

The altar was of stones as they were found, not cut to shape. The law said that a tool used on the stone would defile it.

Two kinds of offering are made. The burnt offering was wholly given to God. The peace offering was shared, and the worshipers ate part of it as a meal in God's presence. So the day held both giving and feasting.

Writing on stone was how the ancient world made a text public. The law is set up where anyone can come and see it.

The list of hearers is deliberate. Women are named. Little children are named. Foreigners living among Israel are named. The law was not the property of priests or of men. Everyone who lived under it had the right to hear all of it, the hard parts with the kind ones.

The battle of Ai and this ceremony sit side by side for a reason. Israel has just learned at great cost what happens when God's word is set aside. Its next act is to stop, worship, and listen to every word.
passages.later:
Moses' command is in Deuteronomy: “And when you have crossed the Jordan, you are to set up these stones on Mount Ebal, as I am commanding you today, and you are to coat them with plaster” (Deuteronomy 27:4). And he had named who must hear the law read: ‘men, women, children, and the foreigners within your gates’ (Deuteronomy 31:12).

Centuries later, after the exile, the people gathered in the same way to hear the law: “So Ezra read it aloud from daybreak until noon” in front of ‘the men and women and those who could understand’ (Nehemiah 8:3).
passages.hard:
Mount Ebal is about twenty miles north of Ai, in country the book has not yet shown Israel taking. Why does the ceremony stand here?

It is a real puzzle, and the old copies of the book show that it was felt early. The ancient Greek translation places this passage a few verses later, after 9:2. One of the Dead Sea Scrolls appears to place a similar account right after the crossing of the Jordan.

Readers have answered in three ways. Some think Israel marched north to Shechem without a fight. The Bible records no conquest of Shechem at all. Some think the passage was set here for its meaning and not for its date, to show that after its obedience was restored Israel's first concern was the covenant, as Moses had commanded for the time when they crossed the Jordan (Deuteronomy 27:2). Critical scholars often take the different placements as a sign that later editors set the passage in at different points.

These notes do not choose. On every view the passage says the same thing about the land. It is received under God's word, read aloud to everyone.
passages.asks: Every word was read, and everyone was there to hear it: women, small children and foreigners. Ask who in your church or your home is treated as if the whole of God's word were not for them. Ask which parts of Scripture you would leave out if the reading were up to you. And notice when Israel did this. Ask whether your first act after a hard season is to stop and listen.
